title: What is your actual workflow for making a complete game with AI?
author: kyazici
selftext:
I’ve been experimenting with AI-assisted game development as a solo developer, and I keep seeing impressive individual pieces: mechanics, UI screens, characters, and short playable demos. However, turning those pieces into a complete, coherent, polished game still requires a lot of planning, iteration, testing, and manual work.

For solo developers who have actually finished and released a game with AI, what workflow do you follow? How do you avoid ending up with a collection of disconnected prototypes, and which parts do you still handle yourself?

comments.author: EverythingBOffensive
comments.body: I talk to it like its a human, ask it questions, make sure it understands what we are talking about and what its looking at. Ask it what it can build in its container and what I need to do to help it work better. Sanity checks and visual proof of the work in its container, show me screenshots of its environment with the game launched in it, build in crash reporters and upgrade them to report as much as possible. Tell the ai you want the tools to be ai friendly, then it will make tools that ai can use with ease, which i've seen it go from shit to damn near beta release in minutes. And think about the ai as a group of temporary workers helping you, they switch even during the same conversation without telling you, so you will need to pin notes and rules on where to begin when they start helping you.

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
The problem is that while you’re still building a reliable pipeline and getting the game to demo quality, AI can start hallucinating and turn the whole project into a mess. You can eventually end up with something completely different from what you originally wanted.

Finishing a complete game is genuinely difficult, whether you use AI or not.

replies.author: EverythingBOffensive
replies.body: it really is. lol. just as you mentioned the prototypes, I build on them constantly but managed to get a good number of "finished" game loops. You have to remind it like its a toddler on how to do stuff. It needs "baseline' operations like follow these steps > look here for help on \_\_\_\_ > make it look like (example) > code it in this way xxxx > don't make these mistakes you did last time xxxx. Lots of pre-work stuff to do before getting it started. when it messes up that means it switched ai assistants on u. so i ask it sometimes if its container did a reset and it will often say yes, so I need stuff from you to continue, otherwise it will go back into la-la land.

comments.author: fluxtah
comments.body:
I think it's more about the game. Since I've been developing my game I took the same approach i do with enterprise projects. I define my ideas in markdown such as game idea, features even ADRs to track architecture. I use GH issues and organise them into milestones which can be many new features or big fixes and adjustments to the last play test. I ensure my AGENTS.md briefly describes the project and my harness tools.

Keeping a project GLOSSARY.md good for jotting down a shared language with the agent.

I generally run one codex thread on a milestone and deliver vertically for play testing frequently so I'm involved in the dev loop 

Tldr; the game idea and ideas that stem from play testing the game are what drives the evolution of it.

I've not released my game on Steam etc yet though so have a website and download to my alpha versions entire deployment pipeline is driven from codex.

Building up a useful harness for the agent for instance so it can read logs etc can help.

Also lots of tests such as frame budget tests and game logic/simulation tests also very useful.

comments.author: JustinGiam
comments.body:
I like to use roadmaps. I ask the AI (Claude) to brainstorm with me and create a roadmap when we're done.

So I'll say, hey lets brainstorm an inventory system for my RPG. I want this this and this, anything obvious I'm missing?

Claude will say: What about this? It could go this way or this way, I recommend this way though.

I approve or deny the AI's suggestions and have it create a roadmap. It looks at the current code and creates a gameplan of code changes in phases and will code 1 phase at a time until the roadmap is complete.

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
That workflow makes sense, but I often run into a problem when working phase by phase. At some point, the project gets stuck, the implementation starts drifting into something completely different from the original design, and the AI begins introducing more and more mistakes.

How do you prevent that kind of drift? Do you update the roadmap or design document as you go, or do you stop and re-plan when a phase starts going off track?

replies.author: JustinGiam
replies.body: I have not had that issue with Claude (Opus or Fable). I have VSCode open along side and inspect changes manually after each phase. If something isn't correct or I want to deviate from the plan slightly, we add a miniphase to make corrections and pick back up at the next main phase. The AI looks at the roadmap (or it should) after each prompt so it stays on track for the most part.

comments.author: peterpolman
comments.body:
Pre AI I hand crafted a POC for my geospatial multiplayer survival game which determined a hierarchical folder structure for various high level components and most of the stack requirements. 

Then I asked Claude to infer an agents.md based on my coding style and architectural setup. I started building out an ADR system for the MVPs scope and game design based on my Obsidian notes. Now when I prompt for GDScript/NodeJS changes Claude knows where to go, how to work and why things are the way they are.

Claude knows how to run the godot binary and is able to create fixtures for my game state so it is able to take screenshots and determine if things look ok.

My game state can be represented in JSON, so I’ve added rules to generate GDScript test scenarios for most systems and their features in the game. When adding new features Claude understands how to extend. These tests are running in CI for my PRs.

I mostly note down ideas in Obsidian and then use Claude to generate issues with acceptance criteria in the Github repo. Then I spawn worktrees per issue and use /grill-me like skills to refine how to build vertical slices for them. This stack of PR’s is auto tested and reviewed and I merely do manual testing on the acceptance criteria before I merge them in.

iOS builds are published automatically using TestFlight so I can test things on my phone after about 10min. Testing locally can be done instant against a dev server and worktrees can run game instances fully parallelised.

I also use Blender MCP to adjust 3d models or generate new low poly models in the same style based on my pixel art UI assets. I did not yet find a way to generate proper pixel art UI assets yet as local diffusion models and SAAS so far disappointed and didn’t match existing art.

I’m having a lot of fun doing this and have no serious goals or anything. I can work on this relatively async and use my phone a lot for initial PRs. 

I hate that AI took my most beloved craft, but I thoroughly enjoy how fast I can play test my ideas. If this ever becomes fun to play I’ll do a rewrite. I have not seen a line of code since I started using AI in this project. I believe that’s fine :)

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
Your approach is very close to what I’m trying to do with my own projects. I start with several game bibles covering the overall vision, gameplay, art direction, technical design, content, and so on, so there is a source of truth from the beginning.

However, I still run into a problem where the implementation gradually drifts away from the documents. When development proceeds phase by phase, the project can get stuck, and the AI starts making technically plausible changes that move the game in a completely different direction.

I’m beginning to think that the missing piece may be a separate “current state” document, together with strict task boundaries and acceptance criteria for every change. Do you maintain a living snapshot of what is actually implemented, in addition to the design documents? And do you only move on after testing, building, and actually playing through the current slice?

replies.author: peterpolman
replies.body:
Only at a very high level, I had a list of systems that were in the MVP scope, which I used to generate a labeled set of GitHub issues I could start working from. 

The ADRs are not design documents, but architectural decision records. In my case this is the reflection of the current state of the game (mostly systems) and is used by Claude when it needs to extend or adjust existing functionality. Code should explain itself (this is in my agent rules), but the layer of ADRs provides the information on how systems actually work together.

The GitHub issue queue is the reflection of what is currently implemented, and I use labels to separate tasks that are in MVP scope or outside of MVP scope. 

Perhaps my current challenge is similar to yours. I now have a whole bunch of nifty systems that can work together. I have a tutorial through which the player can progress and obtain all the tools to do all the stuff, etc. But this isn't fun. In order to make it fun, I need story.

I had some ideas on the theme and challenges the player might need to overcome. Eventually, I had a long voice session with Claude about it to determine an outline of the full progression path in this story:  
\- Early, mid, late game  
\- Which characters we could introduce along this path  
\- What their backstories and incentives are  
\- How the story moves towards the plot over time  
\- Emotional impact of the narrative (there are frameworks for this as well. Think about hero's journey, etc.)

I tell the story through cutscenes, quests and in-game NPCs the player meets. For this, more systems😆. Cutscene Managers, Quest Managers, NPC Dialogue Managers, etc. The input for these systems is in json, easy for both me and claude to work from. Quest beats, cutscene steps, dialog. LLMs are perfect for generating text in the right volume and tone of voice.

I have scoped part of this story for the demo, and I'm currently generating the story inputs and play testing this. I've setup an in game admin panel that allows me to speed up player progression, so I can have access to tools or move through the story really fast to feel if it's coherent. Balancing is for later😇

comments.author: VoidHelm_gg
comments.body: The “collection of disconnected prototypes” problem is probably the biggest AI game dev trap right now. I’ve found that locking the core loop and project structure before letting AI loose makes a huge difference. Curious what others use to keep the agent from constantly reinventing things?

comments.author: CalebKious
comments.body:
I’ve actually shipped games using AI heavily, and I think the biggest mistake is treating development as a sequence of prompts rather than maintaining **one coherent product with a source of truth**.

I run Bezhig LLC as a solo developer. I’ve released **Undead Forever** on iOS/Android, I’m building **FateMMO** on my own custom C++23 engine, and I have other playable projects in development. Codex is involved throughout my workflow, but I don’t just tell it “make an MMORPG” and hope everything eventually connects.

My workflow is roughly:

**1. I own the direction and architecture.**  
Before implementation, I decide what the feature is supposed to accomplish, how the player experiences it, what existing systems it interacts with, and what constraints matter. AI can challenge or improve that design, but I don’t outsource the overall vision to it.

**2. I work inside the existing project, not in disposable prototypes.**  
Once the architecture is established, new features have to integrate with what’s already there. In FateMMO that can mean considering the client, authoritative server, networking protocol, database persistence, ECS, editor tooling, UI, mobile controls, security, and existing tests simultaneously.

That’s where agentic coding becomes much more useful than generating isolated snippets. I want Codex inspecting the repository and understanding the surrounding implementation before changing anything.

**3. I give it bounded problems with concrete acceptance criteria.**  
Instead of “make an inventory system,” it’s closer to: inspect the existing inventory/equipment architecture, implement X behavior, preserve Y invariants, handle these edge cases, add/update tests, build it, and investigate any regressions.

Then I review and actually use it.

**4. Testing is a massive part of making this scale.**  
FateMMO has thousands of automated tests. The more AI I use, the more valuable deterministic verification becomes. Compilers, tests, assertions, protocol validation, database constraints, logging, sanitizers, etc. give the agent objective feedback instead of relying on “this code looks right.”

**5. For visual work, screenshots are basically my feedback loop.**  
This is especially important for UI.

I’ll have Codex implement something, run the game, screenshot the result, then feed that screenshot back with very specific references:

“This panel is too tall.”  
“This spacing doesn’t match the inventory screen.”  
“The hierarchy here is wrong.”  
“This element should align with this reference.”  
“Keep this part, but move the interaction in this direction.”

Then repeat.

I’ve found AI is considerably better at visual work when you give it **the rendered result + a reference + explicit criticism** rather than expecting it to infer your taste from code or a giant initial prompt.

I use a similar iterative process for pixel art, icons, UI assets, animation/VFX frames, etc. AI can get me surprisingly far, but I still curate, edit, reject, composite, and iterate.

**6. I periodically stop adding features and make Codex audit what already exists.**  
Look for duplicated systems, dead code, inconsistent abstractions, security problems, missing tests, TODOs, incomplete integrations, bad error handling, performance issues, and architectural drift.

This is important because AI makes adding features *so cheap* that technical debt can accumulate incredibly quickly if you never make it clean up after itself.

**7. I actually play the game. A lot.**

This is probably the least glamorous and most important step.

AI can tell you that combat is functioning. It can’t ultimately decide whether hitting an enemy feels satisfying, whether progression is tedious, whether a menu is annoying after the 50th use, or whether the game has an identity.

I’ve deleted or substantially redesigned plenty of technically correct AI-generated work because it simply wasn’t fun or didn’t belong.

That’s also the part I absolutely would not hand over: **taste, product direction, final judgment, and deciding what deserves to ship.**

For me, AI didn’t eliminate game development. It dramatically increased the amount of game development one person can realistically do.

The difference between an impressive AI prototype and a finished game is still thousands of boring decisions: integration, debugging, edge cases, balancing, UX, persistence, deployment, platform requirements, security, testing, art consistency, performance, and endless iteration.

My advice would be: don’t build 30 impressive AI-generated pieces and then try to turn them into a game.

**Build one game, establish its architecture and visual language early, and make every subsequent AI task prove that it belongs inside that game.**

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
Thanks for sharing this. The distinction between using AI for implementation while still owning the product decisions is probably the most important part.

I’ve been developing applications for around 25 years, so architecture and integration aren’t new to me, but game development is. I recently shipped my first mobile game, and it made me realize that getting the core mechanic working is only a small part of the job. The real work continues through UX, balancing, edge cases, device compatibility, localization, art consistency, testing, store requirements, and endless iteration.

One thing I still struggle with is drift over time. I start with extensive game bibles covering the vision, gameplay, art, technical design, content, and UI/UX, but the implementation can still gradually diverge. The AI may make several locally reasonable changes while the overall game slowly becomes something else.

Your points about bounded tasks, acceptance criteria, screenshots, audits, and actually playing the game feel like the missing operational layer. How do you maintain the source of truth in practice? Is it mainly the repository and tests, or do you also keep a living architecture or current-state document that Codex updates after each feature?

replies.author: CalebKious
replies.body:
That’s a good follow-up because they’ve identified one of the harder problems with long-running AI development: each individual change can be defensible while the aggregate slowly moves away from the original design. I’d answer their question directly and distinguish between the repo as ground truth for “what exists” and living documentation as ground truth for “what should exist.”

Yes, I use both, and I think the distinction is important:

**The repository is the source of truth for what the game currently IS. The living design/architecture documentation is the source of truth for what it is SUPPOSED to be.**

Tests then enforce the invariants between the two.

For FateMMO, I keep a fairly substantial documentation layer around the codebase: architecture/design documents, system documentation, protocol/database information, implementation notes, player-facing documentation, etc. But I wouldn’t have Codex blindly rewrite a giant game bible after every feature. That can actually introduce another form of drift because now the AI is gradually rewriting the specification to agree with whatever it just implemented.

Instead, I try to separate **intent, implementation and derived documentation**.

High-level product decisions are relatively protected. Things like the game’s identity, major gameplay loops, networking authority model, architectural boundaries, visual language, progression philosophy, etc. shouldn’t silently change because an agent found a locally convenient implementation.

Lower-level documentation can evolve much more freely as the implementation evolves.

For a substantial task, I’ll generally have Codex first inspect the relevant implementation and documentation rather than assuming either one is perfectly current. Then the task gets framed around explicit invariants/acceptance criteria.

After implementation, it builds/tests the result and I can have it reconcile what changed against the documentation. If the implementation legitimately changed the architecture, the corresponding technical docs should change too. If it accidentally violated an architectural rule, the implementation changes—not the rule.

That distinction is extremely useful.

I’ve also found periodic **cross-system audits** more valuable than trying to perfectly document every commit. I’ll specifically ask Codex to investigate something like:

“Compare the current implementation against the documented architecture. Identify contradictions, duplicated concepts, stale documentation, partially migrated systems, violated ownership boundaries, and places where recent implementations have changed the intended design. Don’t modify anything yet; report the discrepancies and recommended resolution.”

That catches exactly the kind of slow drift you’re describing.

And tests are crucial, but tests alone can’t solve it. A test can prove that inventory transactions conserve items or that the server rejects an invalid action. It can’t tell you that you’ve gradually turned the game’s progression into something you never intended.

The other source of truth is honestly **the running game itself**.

I screenshot UI constantly and feed it back with very specific criticism/references. I play through systems repeatedly. If the implementation technically satisfies the specification but the game is becoming visually inconsistent, tedious, confusing or simply less fun, that’s information the repository cannot provide on its own.

One thing I’d be especially careful about with extensive game bibles is **not allowing AI to reinterpret them every time it works**. I’d explicitly distinguish sections that are:

**Invariant / requires my approval to change**  
Core vision, architectural boundaries, art direction, major mechanics, authority/security rules.

**Living / implementation-driven**  
Current APIs, schemas, protocol details, system interactions, tooling, build/deployment details.

**Derived / regeneratable**  
Reference documentation, inventories of systems/content, implementation summaries, etc.

Then Codex knows whether a discrepancy means “update the documentation” or “you’ve violated the design.”

The larger my projects have gotten, the more I’ve realized that AI drift is fundamentally a **governance problem**.

Agents are extremely good at optimizing the task immediately in front of them. Your job is to make sure those locally correct decisions continue serving the same global product.

So I’d keep your game bibles, but make their authority explicit. Combine them with repository-grounded analysis, automated invariants, periodic architecture audits, visual screenshot feedback and actual playtesting.

That has scaled much better for me than trying to create one enormous document that perfectly describes the entire game at every moment.

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
That distinction is extremely helpful, especially the point about not allowing AI to rewrite the design documentation simply to justify whatever it has implemented. I think that is exactly where some of my projects have gradually drifted.

I’ve been treating my game bibles as one general source of truth, but they actually mix three different things: product intent, current technical implementation, and derived content or system documentation. Separating those categories makes much more sense.

I’m going to restructure my workflow so that the high-level design and architectural rules are protected, while the technical documentation can evolve with the code. The repository will represent the current implementation, tests will protect the important invariants, and screenshots and playtesting will validate the actual player experience.

The distinction between “the implementation changed legitimately, so update the documentation” and “the implementation violated the design, so fix the code” is probably the key thing I was missing.

comments.author: BenMakesGames
comments.body:
to get coding done, I:

1. "propose a ticket" (using a skill Claude and I made together) that takes my description, checks feasibility against the code base, asks clarifying questions, and maybe does some "googling"  
2. "write ticket" after I'm happy with how a "propose a ticket" discussion went (if I'm confident some work is very simple, I skip the propose step and start with writing a ticket)  
3. with a fresh context, "implement ticket" pointing to a written ticket. this includes instructions to A. document (ideally inline or docblocks, falling back to dir-scoped markdown files), B. OPTIONALLY write automated tests (100% code coverage is a bad goal to have - only write high-value tests), C. validate the work itself by running the app, interacting, taking screenshots, etc, and D. document trouble points or learned lessons in the ticket before marking that ticket as done  
4. occasionally perform a "retro", which involves going over recently-completed tickets and looking for common pain points; identified issues I agree with I either ask it to immediately fix (if it's small), or "write ticket" for

to get art done, I:

\* use Suno for music  
\* use locally-hosted stable diffusion (ComfyUI), then do a bunch of work myself - I like for-real pixels and low color counts, so I trace the AI work and keep to the palette for the game. I know there are tools out there that might do more of this for me, but I enjoy the excuse to take a break from "coding" to do some art instead, so I'm not rushing to "streamline" this part of my process. (it's also seems kind of fun to have a collection of "concept art" in case I want to share it later, though I haven't actually done this... yet???)  
\* still use [freesound.org](http://freesound.org) for sounds. I tried Suno's sound-generation feature, and it didn't seem great; maybe there's a better one out there. I use Audacity to do edits, mixes (combine a crash + an explosion, for example), and cleanup

for i18n (internationalization), I:

\* store all game strings in JSON, one per language, logically grouping keys by their usage in the game, for example: { "Title Screen": { "New Game": "Nouvelle partie", "Continue": "Continuer", "Settings": "Paramètres", "Quit": "Quitter" } }  
\* any time I add new text, I remind AI to use a subagent to add the translation for the text in every supported language, and to give that subagent context that this is a video game  
\* had Clade code up a special-secret keyboard shortcut that iterates through every language, taking a screenshot for each one and dumping it to disk - good for checking that strings aren't too long for the UI in any language, and for easily getting screenshots for Steam (this required some smarter i18n code so that game states would react immediately to language changes, but I needed that anyway in case someone popped open the settings menu to change their language mid-game, so it was all worth it!)

replies.author: kyazici
replies.body:
This is a really useful breakdown. The separation between proposing a ticket, writing it, and implementing it in a fresh context is especially interesting.

I’ve been starting my own game projects with detailed bibles covering the overall vision, gameplay, art direction, technical design, content, and production. That gives me a source of truth, but I’ve still found that the implementation can gradually drift as the project grows. The AI may complete each phase reasonably well, yet the overall game slowly turns into something different.

Your workflow seems to add the missing execution layer: checking feasibility before coding, creating a bounded written ticket, validating the work through the actual game and screenshots, and using retrospectives to catch recurring problems.

I also like your approach to art. Using AI as a starting point, then manually tracing the results, reducing the colours, and enforcing the game’s palette feels much more realistic for pixel art than expecting a single prompt to produce final assets.

The localization screenshot shortcut is a great idea as well. I’m seriously considering adapting this ticket-based workflow to my own projects. Do you keep a separate living document describing the current state of the game, or is each ticket expected to contain all the context needed for implementation?

comments.author: Normal-Potential-962
comments.body: Your code side already has a source of truth, that's what the AGENTS.md and roadmap answers give you. The art side has none, and that's where the disconnected prototypes usually come from. I ship a low poly tower defence solo; what fixed it was freezing an asset spec first, poly budget plus a fixed palette, then generating every prop against that. Meshy and Tripo get recommended constantly and neither gave me anything usable at that budget, the quads were a mess. Supavoxel is where I landed this year. Blender is still open every day though.
